prompt.context: Our client, OOS (Orrington Office Supplies), is a leading manufacturer of office products. In 1991, they had sales of $275M. They have strong brands, invest heavily in marketing and advertising, and have grown through product line extensions and 4 key acquisitions. OOS is organized into 5 autonomous divisions but shares manufacturing and marketing functions. Shared costs (45% of total) are allocated on a percentage-of-sales method. There are three plants running at a current capacity utilization of 50%.
prompt.question: Analysts predict OOS is a potential acquisition target given its strong balance sheet but weakening earnings. They are publicly traded and have little long-term debt. As a potential investor, how would you improve its profitability?

clarifying_info.a: The U.S. office supplies market grew at 5% CAGR historically. In 1990 and 1991, the market declined at 5%/yr. The superstore channel is becoming increasingly critical, gaining 10 share points in the past 2 years. Superstores typically discount products 30% to small retailers/dealers and are aggressively substituting private label products for traditional brand names.

clarifying_info.q: What does OOS's product line look like compared to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: OOS has a broader product line than competitors: 12,500 SKUs vs. 4,000-5,000 for competitors.
75% wholesalers, 15% superstores, 10% end customers. Staples, Inc. is OOS's largest customer.
The highest-selling product is a high-end branded stapler.

exhibits.title: OOS Sales / Profit Trend
exhibits.shows: A line chart displaying OOS's annual sales and pre-tax profit from the early 1980s through 1991, showing diverging trends over time.
exhibits.data: Sales grew through the 1980s; pre-tax profits declined more steeply than sales in recent years; current (1991) sales ~$275M, pre-tax profits ~$25M.

exhibits.title: Overview of OOS Production Plants
exhibits.shows: A summary table or diagram of OOS's three production plants (Chihuahua, Michigan, New Jersey) showing each plant's location, capacity, and current SKU production at 50% utilization.
exhibits.data: Three plants total; each running at ~50% capacity utilization; Chihuahua plant capacity close to 12,000 SKUs; Michigan ~5,000 SKUs currently produced; New Jersey ~3,000 SKUs currently produced; Chihuahua ~4,500 SKUs currently produced.

exhibits.title: Plant Operating Costs
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing fixed annual plant operating costs and variable annual plant costs for each of the three plants (Chihuahua, Michigan, New Jersey).
exhibits.data: Chihuahua: Fixed $20M, Variable $18M; Michigan: Fixed $15M, Variable $39.5M; New Jersey: Fixed $18M, Variable $25.5M.

framework: 1. Examine OOS recent financial performance: deep-dive into the drivers of declining profits (revenue trends, cost structure, fixed vs. variable costs)
2. Identify capacity consolidation opportunity: analyze the three plants' utilization, SKU production, and feasibility of consolidation
3. Quantify profitability impact of plant consolidation: model revenue effect of SKU reduction and cost savings from closing plants
4. Address qualitative implementation considerations: unions, distribution/warehousing transition, culture/morale, purchasing centralization

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, why have profits declined more steeply than sales?
questions.guidance: The interviewee should identify two insights: (1) The business has a high fixed-cost structure, so declining sales cause profits to fall disproportionately — operating leverage works against OOS as volumes decline. (2) Growth through acquisitions during the 1980s prevented OOS from realizing economies of scale that would normally be expected; instead of scale benefits, acquisitions added complexity and cost.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what are the options for plant consolidation, and which is most feasible?
questions.guidance: The interviewee should recognize: (1) The Chihuahua plant has capacity close to producing all 12,500 SKUs. OOS could close the two U.S. plants and move all production to Chihuahua, OR close Chihuahua and move to U.S. plants. (2) Chihuahua is the most feasible consolidation target because its capacity can accommodate nearly all SKUs (needs to drop only ~500 SKUs from 12,500 to ~12,000). An insightful candidate will ask to see fixed and variable cost data (Exhibit 3) to confirm Chihuahua's cost advantage.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the profitability impact of consolidating all production to Chihuahua (eliminating 500 SKUs).
questions.guidance: The candidate should calculate: (1) revenue loss from dropping 500 SKUs, (2) new total production cost at Chihuahua, (3) net change in pre-tax profit. Strong candidates derive per-SKU variable cost for Chihuahua before building the new cost base.

math.setup: Current: Sales=$275M, 12,500 SKUs, Pre-tax profit=$25M, Total production costs=$136M (Chihuahua $38M + Michigan $54.5M + NJ $43.5M). Consolidate to Chihuahua producing 12,000 SKUs (drop 500 SKUs).
steps: Step 0 — Derive per-SKU variable cost for each plant: Chihuahua $18M / 4,500 SKUs = $4,000/SKU; Michigan $39.5M / 5,000 SKUs = $7,900/SKU; NJ $25.5M / 3,000 SKUs = $8,500/SKU
Step 1 — Revenue impact: Revenue per SKU = $275M / 12,500 = $22,000/SKU. Eliminating 500 SKUs reduces revenue by 500 × $22,000 = $11M. New revenue = $275M - $11M = $264M.
Step 2 — New Chihuahua production cost: Fixed cost $20M + Variable cost ($4,000 × 12,000 SKUs = $48M) = $68M total.
Step 3 — Cost savings: Old total production cost = $38M + $54.5M + $43.5M = $136M. New cost = $68M. Cost reduction = $136M - $68M = $68M.
Step 4 — New pre-tax profit: Old profit $25M - Revenue loss $11M + Cost savings $68M = $82M.
math.answer: Pre-tax profit increases from $25M to $82M, more than tripling. Revenue declines by $11M (4%) while production costs fall by $68M.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative issues should OOS address when implementing the Chihuahua consolidation?

categories.name: Labor & Unions
ideas: If U.S. plant employees are unionized, OOS must negotiate plant closure terms
Severance packages, retraining, or relocation offers for displaced workers
Risk of labor action or work stoppages during transition

categories.name: Implementation Timeline
ideas: Plant consolidation cannot happen overnight; a detailed transition plan is needed
Phased production migration to avoid supply disruptions
Capital investment may be needed to expand Chihuahua capacity for full SKU load

categories.name: Distribution & Warehousing
ideas: Moving from 3 plants to 1 changes logistics network; distribution routes must be redesigned
Warehousing footprint in the U.S. may need to expand to compensate for longer lead times from Mexico
Transition plan needed to avoid stockouts during changeover

categories.name: Purchasing & Supply Chain
ideas: Transition from decentralized local purchasing to a centralized department
Renegotiate supplier contracts under consolidated volumes (potential further savings)
Single-source risk if Chihuahua plant faces disruption

categories.name: Culture & Change Management
ideas: Communicate change clearly and early to prevent morale deterioration
Leadership must manage the narrative around plant closures and job losses
Ensure remaining workforce in Chihuahua is adequately resourced and motivated

categories.name: SKU Rationalization Strategy
ideas: Carefully select which 500 SKUs to eliminate (low-margin, low-volume candidates)
Assess customer impact of dropped SKUs — avoid losing Staples or other key customers
Opportunity to further rationalize beyond 500 SKUs for additional savings

recommendation: OOS should eliminate 500 low-volume/low-margin SKUs and consolidate all production to the Chihuahua plant, increasing annual pre-tax profits from $25M to $82M (more than tripling)
Revenue will decline modestly by ~$11M (4%), but annual production cost savings of ~$68M far outweigh the revenue loss
risks: Labor disputes or union issues at Michigan and New Jersey plants could delay or increase the cost of closure
Concentration of all production in a single plant (Chihuahua) creates operational risk if that facility faces disruption
Loss of 500 SKUs may alienate key customers (e.g., Staples) if eliminated products are important to them
Continued market decline in office supplies and superstore private-label substitution could erode revenues faster than cost savings offset them
next_steps: Develop a detailed implementation and transition plan with timeline milestones
Assess union contracts and begin labor negotiations for Michigan and New Jersey closures
Identify the specific 500 SKUs to be eliminated based on margin and customer importance analysis
Design new centralized purchasing and distribution/warehousing network
Explore further SKU rationalization and shared-cost reduction opportunities
